questions.text: 1.1.1 To what extent do companies involved in the value chain respect the standards elaborated in the 8 fundamental ILO international labour conventions and in the ICESCR  and ICCPR?
questions.comment: Respect for labour rights is generally high in Mongolia, including in downstream cashmere enterprises.

questions.text: 1.1.2 Is freedom of association allowed and effective (collective bargaining)?
questions.comment: Freedom of association is protected by law. The relavant union (MITUF) is represented in a few formal enterprises, others have staff associations, while smaller companies are characterised by paternalistic relations. MITUF is engaged with the employers' association in drawing up baseline salaries for the sector.

questions.text: 1.1.3 To what extent do workers benefit from enforceable and fair contracts?
questions.comment: Written contracts are legally required as of 2022, and are used at least in the larger companies. Employers stress the very low turnover of personnel.

questions.text: 1.1.4 To what extent are risks of forced labour in any segment of the value chain minimised?
questions.comment: Reports of the ILO CEACR mention forced labour issues in other sectors, not in cashmere.

questions.text: 1.1.5 To what extent are any risks of discrimination in employment for specific categories of the population minimised?
questions.comment: Discrimination not mentioned by any interviewees, including MITUF.

questions.text: 1.2.1 Degree of school attendance in case  children are working (in any segment of the value chain)?
questions.comment: School attendance is extremely high for both rural and urban children throughout the lower secondary stage, and still high at the upper secondary stage though lower (66%) for rural males.

questions.text: 1.2.2 Are children protected from exposure to harmful jobs?
questions.comment: Factory work is prohibited for children under 18, and we saw no evidence of it. Nationally (for all economic sectors) 5.4% of girls 5-17 and 10% of boys are involved in labour in hazardous conditions.

questions.text: 1.3.1 Degree of protection from accidents and health damages (in any segment of the value chain)?
questions.comment: Larger factories have in-house systems, but light industry as a sector has a poor record. Workers are not well informed of the risks, but MTUF is organising translation of a major ILO document.

questions.text: 1.4.1 To what extent are remunerations in accordance with local standards?
questions.comment: (for downstream enterprises) Salaries and benefits generally agreed to be in comparison with other light indistries and urban emplyment. (for herding sector) Some concern about conditions for paid herding assistants and their families.

questions.text: 1.4.2 Are conditions of activities attractive for youth?
questions.comment: (for downstream enterprises) Comments against 1.4.1 also apply to youth. (for herding sector) Widespread concerns about attarctiveness of herding for younger generations, especially girls.

questions.text: 2.1.1 Do the companies/institutions involved in the value chain declare adhering to the VGGT?
questions.comment: There are complex politics around acquisition of land for mining, but rights of herders are not well protected in such cases.

questions.text: 2.1.2 If large scale investments for land aquisition are at stake, do the involved companies/institutions apply the 'Guide to due diligence of agribusiness projects that affect land and property rights'?
questions.comment: As for 2.1.1

questions.text: 2.2.1  Level of prior disclosure of project related information to local stakeholders?
questions.comment: In cases of acquisition of rangeland for non-herding purposes, disclosure to herders is low

questions.text: 2.2.2 Level of accessibility of intervention policies, laws, procedures and decisions to all stakeholders of the value chain?
questions.comment: Reasonable knowledge by herders of developments in rangeland policy

questions.text: 2.2.3  Level of participation and consultation of all individuals and groups in the decision-making process?
questions.comment: High participation in bagh assemblies, Rangeland User Groups etc. where rangeland mangement options are debated. Strong civil society participation in national debates on rangeland law

questions.text: 2.2.4 To what extent prior consent of those affected by the decisions was reached?
questions.comment: Please add justification.

questions.text: 2.3.1  Do the locally applied rules promote secure and equitable tenure rights or access to land and water?
questions.comment: The development of rangeland policy and law, though slow, favours equitable access for herders, as do local arrangements

questions.text: 2.3.2 In case disruption of livelihoods is expected, have alternative strategies been considered?
questions.comment: Please add justification.

questions.text: 2.3.3 Where expropriation is indispensable: is a system for ensuring fair and prompt compensation in place (in accordance with the national law and publically acknowledged as being fair)?
questions.comment: Please add justification.

questions.text: 2.3.4 Are there provisions foreseen to address stakeholder complains and for arbitration of possible conflicts caused by value chain investments?
questions.comment: Herders have access to bagh- and soum-level institutions and officials

questions.text: 3.1.1 Are risks of women being excluded from certain segments of the value chain minimised?
questions.comment: Obvious participation of women at all levels of the value chain, including senior- and middle-mangement of formal downstream enterprises

questions.text: 3.1.2 To what extent are women active in the value chain (as producers, processors, workers, traders…)?
3.2.1 Do women have ownership of assets (other than land)?
questions.comment: Household property (campsites, livestock, motorcycles and trucks) is generally registered under the husband's name

questions.text: 3.2.2 Do women have equal land rights as men?
questions.comment: For campsites see above. Rights to graze accrue to the household, but husbands are more likely to participate in discussions on rangeland management

questions.text: 3.2.3 Do women have access to credit?
questions.comment: Most decisions on taking out loans are made jointly, and 14% by the woman alone

questions.text: 3.2.4 Do women have access to other services (extension services, inputs…)?
questions.comment: Access to extension services is limited for both genders

questions.text: 3.3.1 To what extent do women take part in the decisions related to production?
questions.comment: In herding households men are more likely than women to decide on herd and pasture management, seasonal migrations and produce marketing

questions.text: 3.3.2 To what extent are women autonomous in the organisation of their work?
questions.comment: In the herding sector women work as part of the household unit, where men have more say in decisions

questions.text: 3.3.3 Do women have control over income?
questions.comment: Women have less say on household purchases, other than food and clothing

questions.text: 3.3.4 Do women earn independent income?
questions.comment: Nationally, women are more easily employable than men, including in cashmere processing

questions.text: 3.2.5 Do women take part in decisions on the purchase, sale or transfer of assets?
questions.comment: Yes, but with less decision-making power than men

questions.text: 3.4.1 Are women members of groups, trade unions, farmers' organisations?
questions.comment: High membership of cooperatives and rangelend user associations. Where the trade union organises, women are members

questions.text: 3.4.2 Do women have leadership positions within the organisations they are part of?
questions.comment: Women are present as leaders, but less so than men

questions.text: 3.4.3 Do women have the power to influence services, territorial power and policy decision making?
questions.comment: Yes, but less so than men

questions.text: 3.4.4 Do women speak in public?
questions.comment: Yes, but less so than men

questions.text: 3.5.1 To what extent are the overall work loads of men and women equal (including domestic work and child care)?
questions.comment: Clear evidence of inequality in hours worked in the herding sector (average 11.1 vs 9.2 hours)

questions.text: 3.5.2 Are risks of women being subject to strenuous work minimised (e.g. using labour saving technologies…)?
questions.comment: Some labour-saving devices observed, women's and men's work equally strenuous

questions.text: 4.1.1 Does the local production of food increase?
questions.comment: Severe food insecurity is very rare

questions.text: 4.1.2 Are food supplies increasing on local markets?
questions.comment: Severe food insecurity is very rare

questions.text: 4.2.1 Do people have more income to allocate to food?
questions.comment: Cashmere producing households are able to purchase plentiful food

questions.text: 4.2.2 Are (relative) consumers food prices decreasing?
questions.comment: Food price inflation is at manageable levels

questions.text: 4.3.1 Is the nutritional quality of available food improving?
questions.comment: There is widespread concern about lack of dietary diversity in the national diet

questions.text: 4.3.2 Are nutritional practices being improved?
questions.comment: Little evidence for improvement

questions.text: 4.3.3 Is dietary diversity increased?
questions.comment: Little evidence for improvement

questions.text: 4.4.1 Is risk of periodic food shortage for household reduced?
questions.comment: Cashmere herders have options of direct consumption of livestock products or emergency stock sales so are unlikely to face direct food shortage

questions.text: 4.4.2 Is excessive food price variation reduced?
questions.comment: Please add justification.

questions.text: 5.1.1 Do formal and informal farmer organisations /cooperatives participate in the value chain?
questions.comment: Where they were observed, coops and RUAs were strong but only a minority of herders belong to such organisations

questions.text: 5.1.2 How inclusive is group/cooperative membership?
questions.comment: Where they function, coops are open to herders who wish to engage (although some are quasi-coops owned by a small number of shareholders). RUAs are open to herding households in the relevant area.

questions.text: 5.1.3 Do groups have representative and accountable leadership?
questions.comment: The leaderships of coops and RUAs are generally well trusted by herders

questions.text: 5.1.4 Are farmer groups, cooperatives and associations able to negotiate in input or output markets?
questions.comment: Little evidence of effective bargaining on price of inputs or outputs

questions.text: 5.2.1 Do farmers in the value chain have access to information on agricultural practices, agricultural policies, and market prices?
questions.comment: Herders use multiple sources of informatiom

questions.text: 5.2.2 To what extent is the relation between value chain actors perceived as trustworthy?
questions.comment: Trust between value chain actors is generally high, although there is distrust of Chinese-owned factories and their middlemen

questions.text: 5.3.1 Do communities participate in decisions that impact their livelihood?
questions.comment: General satisfaction with participation in coops, RUAs and bagh-level government. Strong civil society participation in national debates on rangeland law

questions.text: 5.3.2 Are there actions to ensure respect of traditional knowledge and resources?
questions.comment: Herders were generally negative on this point

questions.text: 5.3.3 Is there participation in voluntary communal activities for benefit of the community
questions.comment: Strong voluntary participation in neighbourhood activities such as well maintenance, hay harvesting, road maintenance

questions.text: 6.1.1 Do households have access to health facilities?
questions.comment: The great majority of rura people have access to health facilities staffed by doctors at bagh level

questions.text: 6.1.2 Do households have access to health services?
questions.comment: Very high figures for rural women receiving high-quality ante natal and natal care

questions.text: 6.1.3  Are health services affordable for households?
questions.comment: No charges levied

questions.text: 6.2.1 Do households have access to good quality accomodations?
questions.comment: 76% of rural households live in gers. None were observed in less substantial accommodation

questions.text: 6.2.2 Do households have access to good quality water and sanitation facilities?
questions.comment: Human water sources tend to be at a distance from homes. Sanitation is generally rudimentary.

questions.text: 6.3.1 Is primary education accessible to households?
questions.comment: Very high participation, though there are concerns about inadequacy of boarding provision

questions.text: 6.3.2 Are secondary and/or vocational education accessible to households?
questions.comment: Very high participation in secondary education. Good vocational provision at national level

questions.text: 6.3.3 Existence and quality of in-service vocational training provided by the investors in the value chain?
questions.comment: Good provision of training, in a few cases internationally
